idiom_name: plain structs/enums + domain-owned repository trait + TryFrom conversions in the adapter
implementation_notes: Rust's ownership and privacy make the seam unusually clean: the domain crate holds plain structs and enums with smart constructors, the repository is a trait declared by the domain, and the infrastructure crate defines its own row struct - sqlx::FromRow, diesel::Queryable or serde derives belong on that row type, never on the domain type - with conversion impls (impl TryFrom<OrderRow> for Order { type Error = OrderError; ... }) replacing the Mapper class. Conversions are fallible on purpose: TryFrom lets rehydration reject data that would violate an invariant, and mapping database errors into domain errors keeps sqlx::Error out of the model. serde::Serialize on domain types is the same leak in the transport direction and belongs on DTOs.
pitfalls: Derive macros on domain types: sqlx::FromRow, diesel::Queryable or serde::Serialize drag database and wire concerns into the model and defeat the separation even without annotations.
Error leakage: returning sqlx::Error/diesel::Error through the repository trait couples every caller to the driver - map them to domain errors at the adapter boundary.

The orphan rule and privacy shape the design: conversions must live where at least one type is local (usually the adapter), and domain fields must be private enough that only the adapter can construct invalid states.
async traits need care (async_trait or return-position impl Trait); making the repository trait dyn-compatible too early can constrain the whole design.
